data.content_ref: inline:The target is internally self-contradictory: it asserts 'the only consistent Popperian stance is radical skepticism where no theory is preferred for action over another UNLESS one has been falsified and the other has not.' But the target's own mechanism declares that 'any move from has survived to should be used entails a premise that the future will resemble the past,' which is induction. Preferring a non-falsified theory over a falsified one is itself a move from a historical fact ('has been falsified') to a normative action directive ('should avoid this theory going forward'). By the target's own stated criterion, this residual preference smuggles in exactly the same inductive premise it condemns. The carve-out ('unless one has been falsified and the other has not') is a preference-for-action that treats past falsification as a reason for future action—the very structure the target identifies as necessarily inductive. Therefore the target cannot coherently propose even this 'radical skeptical' stance as the sole consistent position, because its own logic brands that stance inconsistent as well. The target either must endorse total paralysis (no preference at all, including not preferring unfalsified over falsified), or it concedes that some non-inductive methodological preferences are possible—collapsing the entire argument.
